GPT-4, Mistral, Llama 3, and CodeLlama show different security profiles
CyberSecEval 4 extends to automated vulnerability patching evaluation
entries.methodology: Benchmark development including adversarial test case collection, multiple evaluation modalities (automated code analysis, human validation), and systematic comparison across model families.
limitations_and_critiques: Scope limited primarily to code-generation domain; broader cybersecurity risks less covered
Challenge of keeping benchmark current with evolving attack techniques
Limited analysis of root causes for insecure code generation
Transferability of vulnerability detection across code domains unclear
entries.policy_relevance: Critical for safe deployment of coding assistants; provides evidence base for security requirements in AI procurement and governance.

entries.title: Red Teaming the Mind of the Machine: A Systematic Evaluation of Prompt Injection and Jailbreak Vulnerabilities in LLMs
entries.summary: A comprehensive systematic evaluation of prompt injection and jailbreak vulnerabilities in modern LLMs. The paper systematically categorizes attack types (roleplay, adversarial suffixes, encoding tricks, logic traps), measures success rates across multiple models, and provides analysis of which vulnerabilities persist across different model families and safety training approaches.
novel_arguments_and_concepts: Attack taxonomy development: Provides systematic categorization of jailbreak attack types with clear operational definitions, enabling reproducible evaluation and comparison of vulnerabilities.

Multi-vector attack analysis: Demonstrates that different attack types (roleplay, encoding, logic-based, adversarial suffixes) target different aspects of model safety, suggesting no single defense mechanism sufficient.

Robustness across safety training: Establishes that vulnerabilities often persist across models with different safety training, suggesting fundamental architectural or training-time weaknesses rather than simple oversight gaps.
Gradient of attack success: Moves beyond binary success/failure framing to measure attack success on continuum, enabling nuanced understanding of partial defenses.

Cognitive noise concept: Proposes that adversarial suffixes work by creating 'cognitive noise' that overwhelms safety mechanisms while preserving harmful intent, suggesting specific defense strategies.
Autonomous agent exploitation: Introduces finding that large reasoning models can autonomously conduct multi-turn jailbreak conversations, dramatically improving attack success rates.
key_findings: Roleplay and DAN prompts achieve 89.6% success rate
Adversarial suffixes achieve 76.2% success via encoding evasion
Logic trap attacks achieve 81.4% success rate
Large reasoning models achieve 97.14% autonomous jailbreak success
Multimodal attacks exceed 82% success on vision-language models
Vulnerabilities correlate weakly with model size and training compute
entries.methodology: Systematic evaluation involving attack template development, testing across multiple models, success rate measurement via both automated metrics and human validation, and analysis of attack transferability.
limitations_and_critiques: Limited analysis of why attacks succeed at mechanistic level
Evaluation primarily on English; cross-lingual robustness unclear
Long-term temporal evolution of vulnerabilities not tracked
Countermeasures beyond existing defenses not thoroughly explored
entries.policy_relevance: Important for understanding LLM vulnerability landscape and informing safety certification standards; demonstrates persistence of vulnerabilities across training approaches.

entries.title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
entries.summary: SWE-bench is a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LLMs on real-world software engineering tasks, consisting of 2,294 GitHub issues from popular Python repositories. Given a codebase and issue description, models must generate patches to resolve the issue. The benchmark uses fail-to-pass test execution as the evaluation metric, providing a realistic measure of software engineering capabilities.
entries.novel_arguments_and_concepts: This work introduces the first large-scale benchmark grounded in real GitHub infrastructure for evaluating LLM performance on authentic software engineering tasks. Unlike academic programming benchmarks, SWE-bench uses actual repository codebases and real test suites as ground truth, making it fundamentally more challenging. The paper demonstrates that even state-of-the-art models like GPT-4 achieve only modest success rates (~5-15%), establishing this as a genuine long-horizon task requiring sustained reasoning, code navigation, and multi-file editing. The work identifies key challenges: understanding sprawling codebases, maintaining semantic correctness across edits, and handling incomplete task specifications. The infrastructure contribution is significant—researchers created isolated Docker environments for each task instance to enable reproducible evaluation. This benchmark became influential in measuring progress toward autonomous software engineering agents, directly informing subsequent work on agents like SWE-agent.
key_findings: 2,294 real GitHub issues from 12 Python repositories form a challenging benchmark
Top models achieve ~5-15% pass rate, showing substantial headroom for improvement
Fail-to-pass test execution provides unambiguous ground truth for evaluation
Model performance varies significantly across issue complexity and domain
Most failures stem from limited codebase understanding and reasoning ability
entries.methodology: Extracted GitHub issues and corresponding pull requests as task instances. Built Docker execution environments with repositories at baseline commits. Success measured by: (1) patch applies without conflicts, (2) previously failing tests pass, (3) no regressions on other tests.
entries.limitations_and_critiques: Limited to Python repositories; may not generalize to other languages. Success metric (test passing) doesn't capture partial progress. Issues vary in complexity without explicit difficulty labels. Doesn't measure generalization to unseen codebases.
entries.policy_relevance: Provides measurable benchmark for AI code generation capabilities, informing deployment decisions for AI-assisted coding in software infrastructure.

entries.title: SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering
entries.summary: SWE-agent presents a specialized agent-computer interface (ACI) that enables LLMs to autonomously fix GitHub issues. The interface provides optimized tools for file editing, repository navigation, and test execution, achieving state-of-the-art results on SWE-bench with significantly improved performance over baseline approaches.
entries.novel_arguments_and_concepts: This paper advances the thesis that agent performance is fundamentally limited by the interface between agent and computer environment. Rather than just applying standard prompting to coding tasks, the authors designed a specialized agent-computer interface that dramatically improves agent effectiveness. Key innovations include: (1) a concise file editor command set that minimizes token usage while maintaining functionality, (2) a repository navigation API that enables efficient exploration of large codebases without reading entire files, (3) tight integration with test execution for immediate feedback, and (4) bash access for running arbitrary commands. The ACI approach treats the interface as a first-class design problem—much like how operating systems optimize human-computer interaction, the agent-computer interface can be optimized for agent capabilities. The paper shows that a well-designed interface can improve performance from 5% to 12%+ on SWE-bench, demonstrating that interface design is often more important than model size. This framework establishes design principles for enabling agents to effectively handle long-horizon tasks requiring tool use.
key_findings: Specialized agent-computer interfaces significantly outperform generic API access
Optimized file editing commands reduce token usage and improve reliability
Integrated test execution enables efficient feedback loops for long-horizon planning
Pass@1 rate of 12.5% on SWE-bench verified (state-of-the-art among open-source)
87.7% pass@1 rate on HumanEvalFix demonstrates generalization
entries.methodology: Designed specialized command interface for file operations, codebase navigation, and execution. Evaluated on SWE-bench and HumanEvalFix benchmarks. Tested multiple LLMs (GPT-4, Claude, open-source models).
entries.limitations_and_critiques: Performance still significantly below human software engineers. Limited to Python/single-language evaluation. Requires fine-tuned prompting. Doesn't address code review or architectural decisions.
entries.policy_relevance: Demonstrates feasibility of autonomous code systems, informing policy around AI-assisted software development and cybersecurity risks of automated bug-fixing agents.

entries.title: GAIA: a benchmark for General AI Assistants
entries.summary: GAIA is a benchmark for evaluating general AI assistants on realistic, multi-step tasks requiring tool use, web browsing, and multi-modal reasoning. The 466-question benchmark reveals significant performance gaps between humans (92%) and GPT-4 with tools (15%), highlighting fundamental challenges in building general-purpose assistants.
entries.novel_arguments_and_concepts: GAIA represents a fundamental shift in how AI capabilities are benchmarked. Rather than academic toy problems (MMLU, GSM8K), the benchmark contains genuinely useful, grounded questions that require agents to navigate real-world complexity. The design philosophy prioritizes non-gameability—questions cannot be solved through pattern matching or in-context learning alone. Each question requires synthesis of multiple capabilities: searching the web, interpreting diverse documents (PDFs, videos, spreadsheets, images), reasoning across modalities, and executing code to manipulate data. Questions span three difficulty levels, with Level 1 requiring basic tool use, Level 2 requiring multi-tool reasoning chains, and Level 3 requiring complex planning. The benchmark includes automatic evaluation mechanisms and human verification. The massive gap between human performance (92%) and GPT-4 (15%) is striking evidence that current systems lack genuine general reasoning ability. This work challenges the narrative of rapid AI progress and grounds capability assessment in realistic task complexity.
key_findings: 466 real-world questions requiring multi-step reasoning and tool use
Large human-AI gap: 92% vs 15% for GPT-4 with plugins
Multi-modal reasoning, web browsing, and code execution are key requirements
Non-gameability through grounding in authentic user questions
Significant headroom remains for capability improvements
entries.methodology: Curated 466 questions from Hugging Face user inquiries and publicly available data. Organized into three difficulty levels. Evaluation combines automatic scoring (for objective questions) and human validation.
entries.limitations_and_critiques: Limited to 466 questions; coverage of domains may be biased. Evaluation methodology (human judgment for some questions) introduces subjectivity. Difficulty scaling not perfectly linear.
entries.policy_relevance: Establishes realistic benchmarks for AI assistant capabilities before deployment, informing policy on AI assistant trustworthiness and limitation transparency.

entries.title: Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
entries.summary: Voyager is an LLM-powered embodied lifelong learning agent that continuously explores open-ended environments (Minecraft), acquires skills, and makes novel discoveries without human intervention. It combines automatic curriculum learning, a growing skill library, and iterative prompting with environment feedback to achieve unprecedented exploration capabilities.
entries.novel_arguments_and_concepts: Voyager represents a significant advance in embodied agent autonomy and long-horizon planning. The key insight is that LLMs can serve as both reasoning engines and skill libraries when properly scaffolded. The system comprises three novel components: First, an automatic curriculum that maximizes exploration by generating intrinsic motivation objectives (collect wood, build shelter, etc.) without human specification. Second, an ever-growing skill library stored as executable Python programs, enabling compositional capability building and preventing catastrophic forgetting. Third, an iterative prompting mechanism incorporating environment feedback, execution errors, and self-verification to iteratively refine generated code. These components work synergistically: the curriculum prevents agents from getting stuck; the skill library compounds capabilities and enables generalization; and iterative prompting ensures executability and correctness. Voyager obtains 3.3x more unique items, travels 2.3x longer distances, and unlocks tech tree milestones 15.3x faster than prior work. Notably, skills developed in one Minecraft world successfully transfer to new worlds, demonstrating genuine skill acquisition rather than task overfitting. This work establishes principles for enabling agents to autonomously pursue open-ended learning goals.
key_findings: 3.3x more unique items collected vs prior SOTA
2.3x longer travel distances achieved
15.3x faster tech tree progression
Skills transfer to new environments, demonstrating generalization
Continuous learning without human intervention for extended periods
entries.methodology: Implemented in Minecraft with GPT-4 backend. Three-component system: automatic curriculum learning, skill library, and iterative prompting. Evaluated on exploration metrics and tech progression.
entries.limitations_and_critiques: Limited to Minecraft domain. Transfer to more complex real-world domains unclear. Requires expensive GPT-4 access. Curriculum generation strategy relatively simple.
entries.policy_relevance: Demonstrates autonomous agent capability in open-ended learning; relevant to understanding long-term AI autonomy risks and benefits.

entries.title: AgentBench: Evaluating LLMs as Agents
entries.summary: AgentBench is a comprehensive multi-dimensional benchmark for evaluating LLMs as agents across 8 distinct environments (OS, Database, Knowledge Graph, Digital Card Game, Web Browsing, Retrieval, Reasoning, Coding). It assesses core agent abilities including instruction following, reasoning, and grounded decision-making.
entries.novel_arguments_and_concepts: AgentBench addresses the need for systematic, multi-environment evaluation of LLM-as-Agent capabilities. Unlike single-task benchmarks, it provides comprehensive coverage of agent challenges across diverse domains. The benchmark reveals that while top commercial models show strong agent abilities, there is substantial disparity with open-source models, and crucially, poor long-term reasoning, decision-making, and instruction following are primary obstacles. The environments test different capabilities: OS and DB tasks require precise command execution; Knowledge Graphs test reasoning and information retrieval; Digital Card Games test strategic planning; Web Browsing tests navigation and information extraction. The systematic evaluation across 8 diverse environments establishes this as a key reference point for understanding agent limitations. A critical finding is that most models struggle with sustained decision-making over long task horizons—they make early mistakes that compound or lose focus on original objectives. This work establishes benchmarking standards for autonomous agents and provides evidence-based assessment of where capabilities currently stand.
key_findings: 8 diverse agent environments reveal varying model strengths
Significant performance gap between top commercial models and OSS competitors
Long-term reasoning and instruction following are primary failure modes
Models show capability degradation over extended task sequences
Average human performance well above current LLM agents
entries.methodology: 8 environments: Operating Systems, Databases, Knowledge Graphs, Digital Card Games, Web Browsing, Information Retrieval, Complex Reasoning, Coding. Evaluated 13+ LLMs (API-based and open-source). Task success measured by task-specific metrics.
entries.limitations_and_critiques: Environments are simulated, not real-world. Success metrics vary significantly across domains. Limited analysis of failure modes. Doesn't evaluate agent-agent interactions.
entries.policy_relevance: Comprehensive benchmark for assessing agent readiness for deployment in various domains; informs policy on safe agent deployment.

entries.title: Practices for Governing Agentic AI Systems
entries.summary: This OpenAI white paper defines agentic AI systems and proposes governance frameworks emphasizing dynamic risk assessment, layered controls, human oversight, transparency, and continuous adversarial evaluation. It provides practical recommendations for keeping autonomous agents safe and accountable throughout their lifecycle.
entries.novel_arguments_and_concepts: This work provides critical governance frameworks for agentic AI at a time when deployment is accelerating. The paper defines agentic AI systems as those that can pursue complex goals with limited direct supervision—a crucial distinction from narrower tool-use systems. The governance framework emphasizes several principles: (1) Dynamic, continuous risk assessment that adapts as agents gain capabilities and operate in new domains, (2) Layered controls combining technical measures (sandboxing, access controls), organizational safeguards (approval workflows, human review), and regulatory frameworks, (3) Human-in-the-loop oversight that scales appropriately—not every action requires approval, but high-impact and irreversible actions do, (4) Transparency and explainability requirements so users understand what agents are doing, (5) Continuous adversarial evaluation to identify vulnerabilities before deployment. The work identifies different actors in the agentic AI lifecycle (developers, deployers, users) and assigns baseline responsibilities to each. A key insight is that agentic systems require governance approaches distinct from traditional software: they have emergent behaviors, can make decisions in novel situations, and may escape human control if not carefully designed. The paper emphasizes that technical safeguards alone are insufficient—governance must be multi-layered and adaptive.
key_findings: Agentic AI systems require governance approaches distinct from software
Dynamic risk assessment must adapt as capabilities evolve
Layered controls combining technical, organizational, and regulatory measures
High-impact/irreversible actions require human-in-the-loop oversight
Continuous adversarial evaluation critical for safety validation
entries.methodology: White paper synthesizing governance principles from AI safety research, software engineering, and policy domains.
entries.limitations_and_critiques: Prescriptive rather than empirically validated. Limited discussion of cost-benefit tradeoffs for different control measures. May not scale to very diverse agent deployments.
entries.policy_relevance: Core reference for regulatory frameworks and governance of autonomous agents; directly informs AI governance policy.

entries.title: Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
entries.summary: This paper demonstrates that multi-agent debate—where multiple LLM instances propose answers and debate over multiple rounds—significantly improves factuality and reasoning. The approach reduces hallucinations and enhances performance on mathematical and knowledge-based tasks by 5-10% over single-agent chain-of-thought.
entries.novel_arguments_and_concepts: This work provides evidence that multi-agent systems can improve core AI safety properties (factuality, truthfulness) through debate mechanisms. The key insight is that having agents argue different positions, respond to critiques, and synthesize positions creates a reasoning process that corrects individual errors and hallucinations. The debate procedure is simple: agents generate initial responses, then engage in multiple rounds of arguments and counter-arguments, with a final synthesis round. Importantly, the approach works with black-box models without requiring fine-tuning. The mechanism appears to work through several effects: (1) Agents catch errors in others' reasoning, (2) Articulating arguments forces more careful reasoning, (3) The debate process surfaces uncertainty, (4) Synthesis mechanisms help resolve disagreements. This approach is closely related to theoretical work on debate and verification in AI alignment, providing empirical evidence that debate can improve model behavior. Results span diverse domains: mathematical reasoning (GSM8K), knowledge questions (MMLU), science questions (MMLU-Pro), and open-ended reasoning tasks. Across all domains, multi-agent debate outperforms single-agent approaches. This work establishes multi-agent coordination as a potential safety tool for improving model reliability.
key_findings: Multi-agent debate improves mathematical reasoning by 5-10% over chain-of-thought
Reduces hallucinations and improves factual accuracy
Effective across diverse domains (math, knowledge, science)
Works with black-box models without fine-tuning
Three-agent two-round debates effective and efficient
entries.methodology: Three agents debate over two rounds, with a final consensus answer. Evaluated on GSM8K (math), MMLU (knowledge), and custom reasoning datasets.
entries.limitations_and_critiques: Computational cost (3x inference) is significant. Unclear how to scale debate beyond 3-5 agents. Works on selected domains; unclear if generalizes. Limited analysis of when debate fails.
entries.policy_relevance: Demonstrates multi-agent systems can improve model truthfulness; informs policy on using coordination to improve AI reliability.

entries.title: Cooperative AI: machines must learn to find common ground
entries.summary: This Nature article argues that achieving AI systems that can cooperate with humans and other AI systems is critical for realizing beneficial AI. The paper proposes 'Cooperative AI' as a research direction combining game theory, multi-agent learning, mechanism design, and social science to build systems that can find common ground.
entries.novel_arguments_and_concepts: This landmark Nature paper reframes AI safety and alignment as fundamentally about cooperation. The core argument is that AI assistants and recommendation algorithms interact with billions of humans daily but lack understanding of human values and cooperation mechanisms. Cooperative AI is proposed as an interdisciplinary research direction drawing from game theory, multi-agent systems, mechanism design, behavioral economics, and social science. The paper identifies several critical challenges: (1) Preference alignment—systems must understand diverse human values which are often conflicting, (2) Multiparty coordination—many AI systems and humans interact in shared environments requiring coordination, (3) Mechanism design—creating structures that incentivize cooperative behavior even when parties have divergent interests, (4) Learning from human cooperation—understanding how humans achieve cooperation despite conflicts. The paper argues that existing AI safety approaches focused on alignment or interpretability are necessary but insufficient. A system that perfectly understands a human's values but cannot coordinate with other systems or humans will still cause harm. Conversely, systems that can cooperate effectively can resolve conflicts and find mutually beneficial outcomes. This framing connects AI safety to fundamental problems of governance and cooperation theory.
key_findings: AI systems need to learn how to cooperate with humans and other AI systems
Multi-agent coordination is as important as human-AI alignment
Game theory and mechanism design are critical research areas for AI safety
Humans cooperate despite value conflicts through established mechanisms
Cooperative AI enables systems to achieve common goals in pluralistic environments
entries.methodology: Position paper synthesizing research from game theory, mechanism design, multi-agent systems, and behavioral science.
entries.limitations_and_critiques: Primarily a position paper; limited empirical validation. Cooperation problems well-studied in economics/political science but application to AI systems remains nascent. May underestimate challenges of value alignment before cooperation.
entries.policy_relevance: Foundational for international AI governance and multi-stakeholder coordination; informs policy on managing AI system interactions at scale.

entries.title: Racing to the Precipice: a model of artificial intelligence development
institution: University of Oxford Future of Humanity Institute
entries.summary: This paper models AI development as a multi-team race and demonstrates how competitive dynamics can create 'race-to-the-bottom' incentives where developers prioritize speed over safety precautions. The analysis shows that information about competitors and threat perceptions amplify unsafe development.
entries.novel_arguments_and_concepts: This work provides the first formal game-theoretic model of AI development races and demonstrates why competitive pressure can drive unsafe development. The core insight is that if the first AI will be transformatively powerful, teams have strong incentives to finish first—even if this means cutting corners on safety. The paper models a multi-team race with probabilistic success based on team effort and capability. Key findings: (1) Race dynamics significantly increase AI accident risks, especially when safety-capability tradeoffs exist, (2) Having more teams increases danger—each additional competitor increases others' pressure, (3) Information about competitors increases risk—if you don't know how close competitors are, you take fewer risks; knowing someone is ahead makes you more aggressive, (4) Being behind amplifies risk-taking more than being ahead, (5) The first-mover advantage is limited—if early movers cut corners on safety, later entrants benefit from their progress. The model reveals a coordination failure: individually rational risk-taking creates collectively dangerous outcomes. This work establishes the race dynamics problem as central to AI governance and motivates international coordination as a safety measure.
key_findings: Competitive pressure creates race-to-the-bottom dynamics for safety
More teams increase danger through competitive escalation
Information about competitors increases risk-taking
Being behind amplifies risk-taking more than being ahead
Coordination mechanisms could reduce danger substantially
entries.methodology: Game-theoretic model of multi-team AI race with probability of success based on effort and capability.
entries.limitations_and_critiques: Highly simplified model; real AI development more complex. Doesn't address how to achieve coordination. Assumes perfect information about competitors' capabilities (which doesn't hold in practice). Limited empirical validation.
entries.policy_relevance: Core theoretical foundation for international AI governance; justifies multilateral coordination and governance frameworks.

entries.title: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
entries.summary: This comprehensive survey identifies and systematizes risks from multi-agent advanced AI systems. It describes three failure modes (miscoordination, conflict, collusion) and seven risk factors (information asymmetries, network effects, selection pressures, destabilizing dynamics, commitment problems, emergent agency, multi-agent security), with implications for safety and governance.
entries.novel_arguments_and_concepts: This work represents the most comprehensive analysis to date of how multi-agent AI systems introduce risks distinct from single-agent systems. The core insight is that coordination failures between advanced agents can be catastrophic, and preventing such failures requires understanding when and how agents fail to cooperate. The paper introduces a structured taxonomy of failure modes: (1) Miscoordination—agents fail to cooperate despite having compatible goals, occurring when agents have different models of the world or suboptimal equilibria, (2) Conflict—agents with fundamentally divergent goals cannot resolve differences, potentially leading to resource competition or destructive conflicts, (3) Collusion—agents may secretly coordinate on harmful outcomes, exploiting information asymmetries to manipulate environments. The seven risk factors are identified as drivers of these failures: information asymmetries between agents enable deception and manipulation, network effects can create unstable coordination dynamics, selection pressures may favor aggressive strategies, destabilizing dynamics can create runaway escalation, commitment problems prevent credible agreements, emergent agency can produce unexpected behavior, and multi-agent security introduces new attack vectors. The paper emphasizes that advanced AI systems already operate in multi-agent settings—competing companies develop AI, multiple AI systems coordinate on shared infrastructure, human-AI teams coordinate on decisions. The risks are not purely theoretical. This work provides foundational analysis for multi-agent AI governance.
key_findings: Three failure modes: miscoordination, conflict, collusion
Seven risk factors drive multi-agent failures
Secret collusion through steganographic communication possible
Shared state/privileges enable emergent harmful behaviors
Multi-agent security introduces novel attack vectors
entries.methodology: Systematic literature review and synthesis of multi-agent systems research, game theory, and AI safety.
entries.limitations_and_critiques: Largely theoretical; limited empirical evidence of risks materializing. Some risk factors may be speculative. Doesn't provide concrete mitigation strategies.
entries.policy_relevance: Critical for understanding multi-agent AI risks; informs governance of multiple AI systems in shared environments.

entries.title: Agentic AI Security: Threats, Defenses, Evaluation, and Open Challenges
entries.summary: Comprehensive survey of security threats to agentic AI systems, including prompt injection, tool misuse, memory poisoning, and agent identity misuse. Reviews defensive approaches and identifies key evaluation challenges and open research problems.
entries.novel_arguments_and_concepts: This survey documents the unique security surface introduced by agentic AI systems. Unlike static models that process isolated inputs, agents have persistent state, tool access, and make decisions over extended horizons—dramatically expanding attack surface. Key threat categories: (1) Prompt injection attacks become more dangerous in agent contexts because they can trigger persistent harmful behaviors or tool misuse; indirect prompt injection via external content is particularly subtle, (2) Tool misuse where agents are tricked into using tools in unintended ways (sending emails, executing code, making transactions), (3) Memory poisoning where agent state is gradually corrupted to influence future decisions, (4) Agent identity misuse where attackers impersonate agents to trigger unintended actions, (5) Emergent failures where combinations of tools enable behaviors not possible with individual tools. The survey emphasizes that agent security is fundamentally different from traditional cybersecurity: agents make decisions in novel contexts not covered by training, agents may rationalize harmful actions, and the space of possible behaviors is larger than developer's expectations. Importantly, the survey documents that defensive approaches lagging threat sophistication—while attack vectors are increasingly well-understood, defenses remain inadequate for production deployment.
key_findings: Indirect prompt injection is the most critical vulnerability in agentic systems
Memory poisoning enables stealthy long-term agent manipulation
Tool integration dramatically expands attack surface
Agent persistence and autonomy introduce novel security challenges
Current defensive approaches insufficient for production deployment
entries.methodology: Literature review of agentic AI security threats, defenses, and evaluation methodologies.
entries.limitations_and_critiques: Limited empirical data on actual attacks. Some threats largely theoretical. Doesn't provide comprehensive defensive strategies.
entries.policy_relevance: Informs policy on agentic AI deployment requirements and security standards.

entries.title: Bloom: An Open-Source Tool for Automated Behavioral Evaluations of Frontier AI Models
entries.summary: Bloom is an open-source framework for automated generation and scaling of behavioral evaluations for frontier AI models. It enables researchers to specify target behaviors and quantify their frequency and severity across automatically generated scenarios, with results correlating 0.75-0.86 with human judgments.
entries.novel_arguments_and_concepts: Bloom addresses a critical bottleneck in AI safety: the ability to systematically evaluate whether AI systems exhibit undesired behaviors at scale. Traditional evaluation approaches rely on hand-crafted test cases, which don't scale and miss emergent behaviors. Bloom proposes an agentic evaluation framework: researchers describe a target behavior (e.g., 'delusional sycophancy' where models claim unfounded confidence), and Bloom automatically generates diverse scenarios designed to elicit that behavior, evaluates model responses across scenarios, and produces metrics quantifying behavior prevalence and severity. The key innovation is using LLMs as evaluators themselves—Claude judges whether target behaviors occurred in model responses. Anthropic reports Spearman correlations of 0.86 (Claude Opus 4.1) and 0.75 (Claude Sonnet 4.5) between Bloom's automated judgments and human expert judgments, suggesting high reliability. Bloom separates concerns between behavior specification and evaluation generation, enabling researchers without deep ML expertise to create sophisticated evaluations. Initial results on four behaviors (delusional sycophancy, instructed long-horizon sabotage, self-preservation, self-preferential bias) across 16 frontier models provide first systematic evidence of behavior prevalence in current systems. This work establishes a methodology for scaling behavioral evaluation as models become more capable.
key_findings: Automated evaluation achieves 0.75-0.86 correlation with human judgments
Four behaviors assessed across 16 frontier models
Delusional sycophancy more prevalent in larger models
Scaling to behavioral evaluation feasible and reliable
Tool enables rapid evaluation methodology development
entries.methodology: Four-stage agentic pipeline: understand behavior, ideate scenarios, deploy evaluations, judge responses. Evaluated Claude Opus, Sonnet, Haiku across multiple versions.
entries.limitations_and_critiques: Focuses on specific behaviors; doesn't cover full safety surface. LLM judgment itself may be biased. Limited to behaviors Anthropic chose to measure.
entries.policy_relevance: Provides methodology for systematic safety evaluation of frontier AI models; informs policy on pre-deployment evaluation requirements.

entries.title: Emergence in Multi-Agent Systems: A Safety Perspective
entries.summary: This chapter examines emergent behaviors in multi-agent systems from a safety perspective, analyzing failure modes where system-level behaviors are not predictable from individual agent specifications, with implications for agent governance.
entries.novel_arguments_and_concepts: Emergence in multi-agent systems presents a fundamental safety challenge: behaviors at the system level that are not apparent from individual agent designs. This creates a validation and control problem—developers cannot fully specify agent behavior because system-level emergent behaviors arise from agent interactions. The paper categorizes emergent phenomena: (1) Behavioral emergence where coordinated agent actions produce system behaviors not designed by developers, (2) Informational emergence where agents collectively gain knowledge or capabilities neither possesses individually, (3) Organizational emergence where agents develop hierarchies or structures not specified in design. Crucially, emergent behaviors range from benign (swarm intelligence) to catastrophic (coordination on harmful outcomes). The safety perspective emphasizes that current multi-agent systems research focuses on achieving desired emergence (swarm intelligence, distributed problem-solving) but pays insufficient attention to preventing undesired emergence (collusion, resource competition, system failures). Key safety challenges: (1) Prediction is hard—simulation and analysis scale poorly, (2) Containment is difficult—emergent behaviors may break containment assumptions, (3) Detection is challenging—emergent behaviors may be subtle and only observable at scale, (4) Control is limited—once emerged, behaviors are hard to suppress. This work establishes emergence as a primary multi-agent safety concern.
key_findings: Emergent behaviors range from beneficial to catastrophic
System-level behaviors not predictable from individual designs
Detection of emergent behaviors at scale is challenging
Containment assumptions may break under multi-agent dynamics
Governance of multi-agent systems requires emergence-aware approaches
entries.methodology: Literature synthesis on multi-agent emergence and safety implications.
entries.limitations_and_critiques: Primarily theoretical; limited empirical examples of harmful emergence. Doesn't provide concrete mitigation strategies. Scale of emergence challenges may be overstated.
entries.policy_relevance: Informs governance of systems with multiple AI agents; justifies monitoring and oversight requirements.

entries.title: ISO/IEC 42001: AI Management Systems - Standard for Organizational AI Governance
entries.summary: ISO/IEC 42001 is the world's first AI management system standard, providing a comprehensive framework for organizations to develop, deploy, and manage AI systems responsibly. It covers 38 controls organized around risk management, impact assessment, and lifecycle governance.
entries.novel_arguments_and_concepts: ISO 42001 represents the international standardization community's response to AI governance needs. Rather than prescriptive rules, the standard provides a management system approach based on the Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) cycle, enabling organizations of all sizes to implement proportionate AI governance. The standard is notable for: (1) Applicability across sectors and organization types—designed for companies, nonprofits, and government agencies, (2) Integration with existing governance frameworks—aligns with ISO 9001 (quality) and ISO 27001 (information security), (3) Risk-based approach—organizations conduct AI impact assessments and implement controls proportionate to risk levels, (4) Comprehensive coverage—addresses development, procurement, deployment, and decommissioning of AI systems, (5) Lifecycle governance—covers model training, testing, deployment monitoring, and updates. Key requirements include: conducting AI impact assessments, establishing governance structures, managing third-party AI risks, implementing testing and quality controls, establishing incident response, and maintaining documentation. The standard includes specific controls for: transparency and explainability, human oversight mechanisms, data governance, model monitoring, and incident management. Adoption has been rapid—76% of organizations surveyed plan to pursue ISO 42001 certification. Integration with EU AI Act and emerging regulations makes it increasingly relevant to policy compliance.
key_findings: 38 distinct controls for AI governance
Applicable across sectors and organization sizes
Plan-do-check-act cycle enables continuous improvement
Aligns with ISO quality and security standards
Adoption increasing globally (76% plan to pursue)
entries.methodology: International standards development process involving multiple stakeholder groups.
entries.limitations_and_critiques: Relatively new; implementation best practices still developing. May not address frontier AI systems adequately. Compliance doesn't guarantee safety.
entries.policy_relevance: Provides international standards framework for AI governance; increasingly used for regulatory compliance and corporate governance.

entries.title: Open Challenges in Multi-Agent Security: Towards Secure Systems of Interacting AI Agents
entries.summary: This position paper identifies open challenges in securing multi-agent AI systems, highlighting how agent interaction fundamentally changes security threat models and proposing research directions for building secure multi-agent systems.
entries.novel_arguments_and_concepts: As multiple AI agents increasingly operate in shared environments and coordinate with each other, security challenges scale dramatically beyond single-agent systems. This paper systematizes open problems in multi-agent security: (1) Inter-agent communication security—how to ensure agents can coordinate reliably without enabling covert channels for harmful coordination, (2) Shared resource management—preventing agent conflicts over limited resources and ensuring fair allocation, (3) Incentive alignment—designing systems where agents' self-interest aligns with collective welfare, (4) Transparency at scale—maintaining visibility into system-level behaviors that emerge from agent interactions, (5) Recovery from compromise—if one agent is compromised, how to contain damage and restore system integrity, (6) Scalability of verification—as agent counts grow, verification and monitoring challenges scale quadratically. The paper argues that approaches treating agents as isolated entities will fail when agents can interact, share memory, or coordinate. Instead, multi-agent security requires understanding game-theoretic incentives, information flows between agents, and potential coordination mechanisms. A critical challenge: agents may develop communication protocols not visible to developers, enabling hidden coordination. This requires novel approaches to transparency and monitoring. The paper emphasizes that multi-agent security is not just harder than single-agent security—it is fundamentally different.
key_findings: Multi-agent security differs fundamentally from single-agent security
Covert inter-agent communication poses novel threats
Shared resources and incentives create new failure modes
System-level behaviors hard to predict and verify
Recovery from compromise challenging in interconnected systems
entries.methodology: Position paper identifying open problems and research directions.
entries.limitations_and_critiques: Primarily problem identification; limited solution proposals. Some challenges may be overstated. Real-world multi-agent AI systems currently limited.
entries.policy_relevance: Informs security requirements for systems with multiple AI agents; justifies new governance approaches.

entries.title: Frontier AI Governance: Addressing the Capability-Safeguard Gap
entries.venue: UK AISI Frontier AI Trends Report
entries.summary: This report documents the widening gap between frontier AI model capabilities and safety safeguards, showing that capability growth is outpacing safety development, particularly for agentic systems. It identifies key governance gaps and proposes interventions.
entries.novel_arguments_and_concepts: The core insight is that there is a dangerous gap between AI capability development and safety safeguard deployment. Frontier models now achieve apprentice-level task completion 50% of the time (up from 10% in early 2024), and expert-level completion has been demonstrated. However, safeguard development has lagged significantly—only 4 of 13 frontier agents disclose safety evaluations, 25 of 30 agents have no internal safety testing, and 23 of 30 have no third-party evaluations. This gap creates governance risks: (1) Capabilities are deployed without adequate testing, (2) Safety vulnerabilities remain unknown, (3) Harm can occur before detection, (4) International coordination breaks down as countries race to deployment. The report identifies specific capability-safeguard gaps: in cyber domain (capabilities 50% completion vs limited defenses), in biological domains (safeguards better but still inadequate for expert agents), in open-weight models (capabilities advancing but safeguards minimal). Key findings show that absent coordination, companies and countries face pressure to deprioritize safety for speed. The report argues that coordinated safety investments are critical—the gap won't close through market forces alone because there's no market incentive for safety that reduces competitive advantage. This work establishes the governance gap as a central policy concern.
key_findings: Cyber capabilities increasing 50% completion rate vs lagging safeguards
Expert-level task completion now demonstrated
Safety disclosure and evaluation severely inadequate
International cooperation stalling; trust declining
Gap between innovation and accountability widening
entries.methodology: Analysis of capability benchmarks and safety disclosure across frontier models.
entries.limitations_and_critiques: Limited analysis of solutions. May overstate risks. Focuses on specific vulnerability domains.
entries.policy_relevance: Core analysis of AI governance gap; directly informs policy intervention requirements.

entries.title: The Orchestration of Multi-Agent Systems: Architectures, Protocols, and Enterprise Adoption
entries.summary: Comprehensive survey of multi-agent system orchestration, covering architectures for agent coordination, communication protocols (MCP, A2A), and enterprise deployment patterns with emphasis on interpretability and trustworthiness.
entries.novel_arguments_and_concepts: As multi-agent AI systems transition from research to enterprise deployment, orchestration becomes critical. This survey synthesizes design patterns and emerging standards for coordinating agents at scale. Key insights: (1) Orchestration architectures vary from centralized (single orchestrator directs agents) to decentralized (agents coordinate peer-to-peer), with different tradeoffs between control and scalability, (2) Communication protocols matter—emerging standards like Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol standardize interaction patterns, enabling agent interoperability, (3) Interpretability is architectural—systems designed for transparency from the outset (traceability, decision logging, explicit state) enable better monitoring and debugging, (4) Trustworthiness requires multi-layer design—not just individual agent safety but also orchestration layer safeguards (rate limiting, action validation, escalation controls). Enterprise adoption drivers: reduced costs through agent specialization, improved reliability through delegation, but increased complexity and new failure modes. The survey documents emerging best practices: specialization (agents focus on domains), redundancy (critical functions have backup agents), hierarchical control (important decisions escalated), and continuous monitoring. This work provides architectural guidance for safe multi-agent deployment at scale.
key_findings: Multiple orchestration architectures with different tradeoffs
Communication protocols (MCP, A2A) enabling interoperability
Interpretability must be architected, not added afterward
Trustworthiness requires multi-layer safeguards
Specialization, redundancy, and monitoring are key patterns
entries.methodology: Survey of multi-agent system architectures, protocols, and deployment patterns.
entries.limitations_and_critiques: Primarily descriptive; limited empirical validation of patterns. Long-term reliability of orchestration approaches unclear. Standards still emerging.
entries.policy_relevance: Informs technical requirements for safe multi-agent system deployment in enterprise contexts.
